name: 8. Searching & Sorting Algorithms
title: Searching, Sorting & Parametric Search Algorithms
description: Master foundational and advanced searching and sorting algorithms in Java: linear search, iterative and recursive binary search, lower and upper bounds, rotated sorted array search, binary search on answer (monotonic predicates), elementary sorting (bubble, selection, insertion), efficient divide-and-conquer sorting (merge sort, quicksort, heap sort), non-comparison linear sorting (counting, radix, bucket sort), stability invariants, and Java standard library sorting APIs (Arrays.sort and Collections.sort).
topics: What Is Searching: Search Keys, Unsorted vs Sorted Collections & Strategy Trade-offs
What Is Sorting: Ascending vs Descending, Comparison vs Non-Comparison Lower Bounds (Ω(n log n))
Linear Search: Sequential Scanning, Best/Avg/Worst Cases & When to Use
Binary Search: Divide & Conquer Halving, Loop Invariants & Mid Overflow Prevention (low + (high - low) / 2)
Recursive vs Iterative Binary Search: Auxiliary Stack Frames vs O(1) Iteration
Binary Search Prerequisites: Sorted Invariants, Consistent Comparators & RandomAccess Lists
Binary Search on Answer (Parametric Search): Monotonic Predicates & Minimum/Maximum Feasibility Bounds
Worked Parametric Search: Minimum Ship Capacity Within D Days (O(n log R))
Lower Bound & Upper Bound: Half-Open Intervals [low, high), First >= Target vs First > Target
Counting Occurrences & Frequency Range: upperBound(x) - lowerBound(x) in O(log n)
Search in Rotated Sorted Arrays: Distinct Values Pivot Logic vs Duplicate Handling Degradation
Bubble Sort: Adjacent Inversion Swapping, Early-Exit Flag Optimization & Stability Proof
Selection Sort: Unsorted Suffix Minimum Selection, O(n) Swaps & Instability Proof
Insertion Sort: Sorted Prefix Element Insertion, Adaptive O(n) Best Case & Online Data Feasibility
Merge Sort: Divide-and-Conquer Recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n), Stability Preserving <= Merge & O(n) Buffer
External Merge Sort: Multi-Way Run Merging for Datasets Larger than Physical RAM
Quick Sort: Lomuto Partitioning, Pivot Selection Strategies & Quicksort Recurrence Analysis
Quicksort Optimizations: Median-of-Three, 3-Way Partitioning (Dutch National Flag) & Small Subarray Cutoffs
Heap Sort: Complete Binary Trees in Arrays (2i+1, 2i+2), Max-Heapify O(n) Build & Guaranteed O(n log n)
Counting Sort: Non-Comparison Frequency Tallies, Cumulative Prefix Positions & Negative Offset Support
Radix Sort: Least Significant Digit (LSD) Passes, 4-Byte Signed Shift Bitmasks (>>> shift & 0xFF)
Bucket Sort: Uniform Interval Distribution [0, 1), Individual Bucket Insertion Sort & Average O(n+k)
Stable vs Unstable Sorting: Key-Tie Preservation Invariants in Multi-Attribute Database Records
In-Place vs Out-of-Place Sorting: Auxiliary Memory Bounds & Recursive Stack Overhead Accounting
Complete Sorting Complexity Matrix: Best, Average, Worst & Space Trade-offs Across 9 Algorithms
Java Arrays.sort(): Dual-Pivot Quicksort for Primitives vs Adaptive Stable TimSort for Objects
Java Collections.sort(): List Sorting, Custom Comparators & RandomAccess vs LinkedList Traversal
Common Interview Archetypes: Koko Eating Bananas, Aggressive Cows, Rotated Arrays & First/Last Positions
Practical Laboratory Exercises (5 Labs), 6 Independent Assignments & SearchSortToolkit Mini-Project

quiz.question: Which searching algorithm works without requiring sorted input?
quiz.explanation: Linear search inspects elements sequentially one by one, functioning correctly on unsorted and sorted datasets alike.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search?
quiz.explanation: In the worst case (target at the very end or absent), linear search must examine all n elements, taking O(n) time.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?
quiz.explanation: Binary search repeatedly halves the search space, reducing an interval of size n to 1 in at most log2(n) steps.

quiz.question: What is required for ordinary binary search to produce guaranteed correct results?
quiz.explanation: Binary search relies on elements being sorted so it can safely eliminate half of the remaining candidates after each comparison.

quiz.question: Which search algorithm finds the index of the first element greater than or equal to a target?
quiz.explanation: Lower bound returns the first index i where array[i] >= target, or array.length if no such element exists.

quiz.question: Which sorting algorithm is based on the divide-and-conquer paradigm?
quiz.explanation: Merge sort divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts them, and merges the sorted halves in linear time.

quiz.question: Which sorting algorithm is stable in its standard implementation?
quiz.explanation: Insertion sort preserves the relative order of equal keys because it only shifts elements strictly greater than the key.

quiz.question: Which sorting algorithm typically requires O(n) additional auxiliary array memory?
quiz.explanation: Standard array merge sort requires an auxiliary buffer of size n to merge two sorted subarrays.

quiz.question: Which sorting algorithm repeatedly builds a sorted prefix by inserting the next element into its correct place?
quiz.explanation: Insertion sort takes the next unsorted element and shifts larger elements to the right to insert it at its sorted position.

quiz.question: Which sorting algorithm uses a binary heap data structure?
quiz.explanation: Heap sort builds a max heap in O(n) time, then repeatedly extracts the root maximum to achieve in-place O(n log n) sorting.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of conventional quicksort?
quiz.explanation: If the pivot consistently partitions into 0 and n-1 elements (e.g. sorted input with last-element pivot), quicksort degrades to O(n²).

quiz.question: Which non-comparison sorting algorithm is particularly efficient when integer values fall within a small range k?
quiz.explanation: Counting sort tallies element frequencies in an array of size k, achieving O(n + k) linear-time performance.

quiz.question: Which technique sorts numbers or strings digit by digit from least significant to most significant digit?
quiz.explanation: LSD Radix sort performs multiple stable sorting passes on individual digit positions, achieving O(d(n + b)) time.

quiz.question: Which Java standard library class provides the static Arrays.sort() method?
quiz.explanation: Arrays.sort() is a static utility in java.util.Arrays for sorting primitive and object arrays.

quiz.question: Which Java utility method sorts a List collection?
quiz.explanation: java.util.Collections.sort() sorts List implementations using natural ordering or a provided Comparator.

quiz.question: In binary search on answer problems, what property must the feasibility predicate function satisfy?
quiz.explanation: The feasibility condition must be monotonic (e.g. false, false, ..., true, true) so that binary search can locate the transition threshold.

quiz.question: In a rotated sorted array with distinct values, how does modified binary search eliminate half the search space?
options: By checking whether numbers[low] <= numbers[mid] to determine which half is normally sorted
By checking if the array length is even
By performing linear search on both halves
quiz.explanation: At least one half of the rotated interval is always strictly sorted. If numbers[low] <= numbers[mid], the left half is sorted; otherwise the right half is sorted.

quiz.question: In bucket sort with insertion sort in each bucket, what is the worst-case time complexity if all elements fall into one bucket?
quiz.explanation: If all n elements cluster into a single bucket, sorting that bucket with insertion sort incurs its worst-case O(n²) time.

quiz.question: Does Java guarantee that Collections.sort() is stable for object elements?
options: Yes, stability is guaranteed by the API specification
Only when sorting in descending order
quiz.explanation: Java guarantees stable sorting for object collections; equal elements never change relative positions.

quiz.question: How can the exact count of occurrences of target in a sorted array be computed in O(log n) time?
quiz.explanation: Because lower bound points to the first occurrence and upper bound points immediately after the last occurrence, count = upperBound - lowerBound.
